title: TCP/IP Model
summary: The TCP/IP model is a four layer description of how networked communication is organised: the link layer that moves frames across a local medium, the internet layer that routes packets between networks, the transport layer that provides end to end delivery through TCP or UDP, and the application layer that carries protocols such as HTTP, DNS and SMTP. It is a practical model derived from the protocols the internet actually runs, in contrast to the seven layer OSI reference model, which is a more abstract teaching framework. In a real environment the model is a troubleshooting and analysis tool: it tells you which addresses and artefacts to inspect at each stage, and it explains why a packet capture exposes different fields than an application log. The common mistake is treating the layers as strict software boundaries, since real implementations combine or bypass them and encryption such as TLS obscures where application data begins.

beginner.definition: The TCP/IP model is a way to describe how computers send data across a network. TCP/IP stands for Transmission Control Protocol and Internet Protocol. It groups the many jobs involved into four simple layers. Each layer passes its work to the next one, like a ladder.
beginner.whyItMatters: When something breaks, you need a clear order for checking it. The model tells you to test the cable, then the address, then the connection, then the application. That saves time and stops guesswork. It also helps you understand where a control such as a firewall or a proxy really sits. Without this shared map, teams argue about symptoms instead of finding the cause.
howItWorks: Your program creates the message, such as a request for a web page.
The transport layer breaks it into pieces and adds port numbers for the two programs.
The internet layer adds source and destination addresses so routers can forward each piece.
The link layer puts every piece into a frame for the local network and sends it out.
At the other end the layers are unwrapped in reverse order until the message appears.
Each layer on the receiving side checks its own work and can ask for a missing piece again.
beginner.example: Picture a postal system. You write a letter and put it in an envelope with the name of the department. The post office adds the street address and the city so sorting machines can route it. A van carries the bag between buildings on the same street. At the destination the bag is opened, the envelope is checked and the letter reaches the right desk. The TCP/IP model describes those same stages for network data.
takeaways: The TCP/IP model has four layers: link, internet, transport and application.
It gives you a fixed order for troubleshooting, from the cable upwards to the application.
Real systems do not respect the layers perfectly, because encryption and software blend them.

objectives: Name the four layers of the TCP/IP model and the job of each one.
Explain how data is wrapped as it moves down the layers and unwrapped on receipt.
Describe how the model differs in purpose from the OSI reference model.
Use the model to choose which artefact to inspect during troubleshooting.
Identify where a firewall, proxy or encryption layer sits in the model.
Explain why real implementations do not follow the layers strictly.
